passage:
Monday. At the park, Yash announced a club called the Thunder Owls. “Secret handshake: two knocks, one flap.” Leela practised it until her wrist hurt. Two more children were made members after they got it right.
Thursday. A boy named Mihir asked to join. “What's the handshake?” Yash asked. Mihir fumbled it, and Yash shrugged. “Not yet.” The others looked at their shoes. Leela said nothing.
Sunday. Leela taught Mihir the handshake behind the swings, twice. When he did it right, she went to Yash. “He knows it.” Yash hesitated, then flapped both arms. “Okay. Welcome, Owl.”

qa.q: What was the Thunder Owls' secret handshake?
qa.a: The handshake was two knocks and one flap.

qa.q: What might Leela have been feeling when Leela said nothing on Thursday while Mihir was turned away?
qa.a: Leela probably felt uneasy and uncertain about speaking up, since the others looked at their shoes and Leela taught the handshake secretly three days later.

qa.q: What choice did Leela make on Sunday, and what did it change?
qa.a: Leela taught Mihir the handshake and then spoke to Yash about him, so the ritual that marked who belongs was used to let Mihir in.

qa.q: How might Mihir have seen the club after fumbling the handshake on Thursday?
qa.a: Mihir may have felt shut out and embarrassed, so being taught the handshake by Leela probably felt like being welcomed after all.

grounding: Children invent a club, handshake and rules, and the ritual marks who belongs and who does not.

passage: “We had a club when I was ten,” said Mausi Manjula. “The Seven Stars. We met behind the water tank in our colony. To join, you hopped on one leg round the tank and swore on a paper star. Our leader, Pinky, said a proper club needed exactly seven, so no eighth member. Then Gurpreet moved into the flat above ours. He was so eager! He hopped so well round the tank. But Pinky said, ‘Seven only.’ I remember Gurpreet's face. After that, the rest of us made our own rule: anyone could hop.” She laughed. “We dropped the number and called ourselves The Stars.”

qa.q: Where did the Seven Stars meet?
qa.a: The Seven Stars met behind the water tank in their colony.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet have been feeling when Pinky said, “Seven only”?
qa.a: Gurpreet was probably hurt and disappointed, since Gurpreet had hopped so well and was still turned away.

qa.q: What was the turning point that changed the club?
qa.a: The rest of the children decided that anyone could hop, and dropped the number, so the club no longer left newcomers out.

qa.q: What might Pinky have been thinking when Pinky insisted that the club needed exactly seven?
qa.a: Pinky may have wanted the club to feel special and firm, and did not see how much the fixed number would hurt someone new.

grounding: Children invent a club with a ritual that marks who belongs, and an elder recalls how it left someone out.

passage: Monday: under the stairs at school, Ujjwal, Keerthana and Manav invented the Tiger Club. The handshake was two slaps, a fist bump and a growl. Rule one: nobody tells the password. Ujjwal felt ten feet tall. Thursday: a new boy, Arif, asked to join. Keerthana said, 'Tiger Club is only three.' Arif walked off, and Ujjwal felt a strange mix of pride and guilt. The next Monday: Ujjwal saw Arif eating alone again. At the stairs, Ujjwal said, 'What if we had a joining test? Like, he has to growl.' Manav rolled his eyes but agreed. Arif growled so loudly that a teacher looked round. The Tiger Club was four.

qa.q: What was the Tiger Club handshake?
qa.a: Two slaps, a fist bump and a growl.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when Arif walked off on Thursday?
qa.a: A strange mix of pride in the club and guilt at shutting Arif out.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do to let Arif in, and why did it work?
qa.a: Suggested a joining test, a growl, so Arif could belong without the club losing its special ritual.

qa.q: What was it like for Arif to be turned away and then let in?
qa.a: He likely felt rejected and lonely at first, then happy and accepted, growling loud enough for a teacher to look round.

grounding: Children invent a club ritual that marks who belongs, and later stretch it to include a newcomer.

passage: Parul, you and your friends have a secret handshake? Your Thomas uncle had one too, in Kottayam, sixty years ago. Five of us, the Mango Tree Gang. To join, you had to climb to the third branch and eat a raw mango without making a face. Our sign was two taps on the nose. We thought we were kings. Then a boy called Varghese moved into our street. He couldn't climb because of his leg brace. We said rules are rules. For a whole summer he watched us from his gate. One evening I climbed down and brought him a mango. I tapped my nose twice. The others were angry for a day. After that, the rule was: climb or be carried. Remember that when you make your rules.

qa.q: What was the Mango Tree Gang's sign?
qa.a: Two taps on the nose.

qa.q: How might Varghese have felt watching from his gate all summer?
qa.a: Probably lonely and left out, shut out by a rule he couldn't meet.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed the gang, and why?
qa.a: Young Thomas bringing Varghese a mango and giving him the sign; it showed the ritual could welcome, not only exclude.

qa.q: How did the other gang members react to the new rule?
qa.a: They were angry for a day, protective of their rules, but then accepted 'climb or be carried'.

grounding: An uncle recalls a childhood gang whose joining ritual marked who belonged, until he stretched it to include a boy left out.

passage: The Secret Stitchers had one rule: every Saturday at four, under the jamun tree behind Block C, each member showed one thing she had sewn, and they all said, 'Needle, thread, friends ahead!' This Saturday it poured. The tree was dripping, and Sharmila's mother wouldn't let four muddy girls into the flat. Simran looked ready to cry; the club had never missed a week. Then Sharmila had an idea: the staircase landing. They squeezed in between the fourth and fifth floors, knees touching, and showed their pieces: a pencil pouch, a crooked heart, a doll's scarf. The lift man peered at them. They whispered the chant so nobody else would hear, which made it feel even more secret and even better.

qa.q: Where did the Secret Stitchers usually meet?
qa.a: Under the jamun tree behind Block C.

qa.q: Why did Simran look ready to cry?
qa.a: She was upset and worried because the rain threatened to make the club miss a week for the first time.

qa.q: How did Sharmila keep the ritual going despite the rain?
qa.a: By finding the staircase landing, so they could still show their pieces and say the chant together.

qa.q: How might the lift man see the four girls on the landing?
qa.a: He probably found them puzzling or amusing, not knowing the whispered chant marked who belonged to their club.

grounding: Children keep their club's made-up ritual going through bad weather, because it marks who belongs.

passage: On the terrace of Block C in their Chennai colony, Vijay, Chandrika and Imran invented the Tank Club, named after the water tank they sat under. The rules: meet at five, the password is "rasam", and the handshake is two slaps, a thumb twist and a pretend sneeze. Vijay practised the sneeze in the mirror at home. On Thursday a new boy, Joel, climbed the stairs and asked to join. The three looked at one another. Chandrika said, "You have to know the password." Joel didn't. He stood there awkwardly, then went back down. Vijay felt big for a moment, then strangely bad. The next day he taught Joel the handshake behind the stairwell, sneeze and all.

qa.q: What was the Tank Club's password?
qa.a: The password is "rasam".

qa.q: What did Vijay feel after Joel went back downstairs?
qa.a: He felt important for a moment, then strangely bad, as if the club's rule had been unkind.

qa.q: How could the Tank Club keep its fun without shutting others out?
qa.a: They could keep the handshake and password but teach them to newcomers like Joel, as Vijay did, so the ritual welcomes instead of excludes.

qa.q: What was it like for Joel on the terrace without the password?
qa.a: Joel probably felt awkward and left out, facing a club where a made-up word decided who belonged.

grounding: Shows children inventing a club with a password and handshake that marks who belongs and who does not.
